newsitem.title: UK: UK oil firms hoard petrol before budget tax hike.
newsitem.headline: UK oil firms hoard petrol before budget tax hike.

text.p: British motorists can expect an increase in petrol prices even before the government's November budget as oil companies start to hoard supplies in anticipation of a duty increase, oil traders and analysts say.
Signs have aleady emerged that oil companies are preparing to stock up with fuel taxed at pre-budget levels in order to cash in on higher pump prices after the budget.
"It's usual to see these kind of moves at this time of year," said a trader for one of Britain's top petrol retailers.

An indication of the trend is that prices for oil to be delivered in November are higher, by a wider than normal margin, than for December deals. The differential for November has climbed $2.50 a tonne this week to around $16 a tonne and is set to widen out further, traders said.

Because of a combination of higher taxes and wholesale gasoline prices at post-Gulf War highs, British pump prices are at record highs and may go higher even before the budget is announced on November 26. Prices at the pump for a gallon of premium unleaded gasoline stand around $4.16.
But because of an intense price war among British retailers, profit margins for the retailers are at their lowest levels, the Petrol Retailers' Association said.
"Excluding duty and VAT, the margins are at their lowest levels in EC records and the margins are the lowest in Europe," said Paul Sykes, president of the Petroleum Retailers Association.
Sykes and others have no doubt that the pump prices will rise but that the high costs will not deter British motorists from filling up.
"Prices would have to more than double to cut into demand. But with 75 percent of the pump price taken up by duties and VAT, the margins for retailers are still very low," Sykes said.
The British government already has committed itself to raising excise duty of gasoline by five percent annually plus the rate of inflation which currently runs at 2.9 percent.
Despite strong competition on the forecourt, any tax increases are expected to be passed straight to the consumer.

"Even if (oil traders) buy the odd extra cargo that they wouldn't otherwise have bought, that could send prices up throughout Europe," said Peter Regnier of industry consultants Oil Price Assessments Ltd (OPAL).
"Duty is the one thing that (oil companies) endeavour to recover no matter what."
A 7.9 percent increase in excise duty would translate to a pump price hike of 3.2 pence a litre on premium unleaded, OPAL estimates.
For oil companies, the rewards of storing duty-paid fuel for sale after the budget would be immense.
The additional revenue on pump sales would be some $50 to $60 a tonne, or around one quarter of current European gasoline spot prices.
"As usual we'll see a lot of anticipated purchases of gasoline cargoes driven by the expectation of this kind of duty increase," said OPAL's Regnier.
But with a general election expected next spring, Regnier said the government may put its "green" policies on hold in an effort to butter up motorists.
"Maybe this year (the oil traders) will be caught out," he said. "With an election coming up anything could happen,"
